:::: {.slide-outcomes}

::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. [**Explain** the two main purposes of grouping]{.slide-bullet}:
   - Making direct comparisons between groups,
     e.g., observations in group A tend to have higher values
     than those in group B.
   - Avoiding incorrect generalizations,
     e.g., there could be an overall positive trend
     when all observations are viewed together,
     while the data for individual groups displays negative trends
     or no trend at all.
2. [**Evaluate** which grouping strategy is the most suitable in a specific
   context]{.slide-bullet}:
   - Color (optionally combined with shape) distinguishes groups while keeping
     observations close together on shared positional scales for comparing values.
   - Grouping by position gives each category its own lane
     for comparing values of another variable.
   - Faceting is often effective
     when comparing the pattern or trend of a group
     to those of other groups
     since it shows the observations for each group separately.
3. [**Apply** grouping strategies using color, shape, and position (including facets)
   to visually distinguish between categories]{.slide-bullet}
:::

## Why grouping matters

So far, you have created declarative visualizations by representing observations
as point **marks** on a canvas, using position and color to represent quantitative variables.
This is the foundation for all the visualizations we will make,
but it is rarely sufficient on its own to give a complete picture of the data.
In particular, real-world datasets might show overall trends
that disappear or change when individual groups are explored more closely.
The goal of grouping is to distinguish between groups by basing the visual
appearance or placement of points in a chart on the value of a categorical variable.
Let's see this in action in the following exercise.

::::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

Before making a chart, make a prediction:
would countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers
tend to have higher or lower life expectancy?
What makes you expect that?

We will [investigate a country-level dataset containing
the percentage of heavy drinkers
and the average remaining life expectancy at age 65]{.slide-bullet}.^[Sources: Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 (GBD 2021) Results; [World Bank country and lending groups](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups).]
In our scatterplot, each point represents a country.
The x-axis shows the percentage of heavy drinkers,
and the y-axis shows the average number of years
a person reaching age 65 can expect to live beyond that age.^[Retirement age differs between countries. We have used age 65 as it is close to the average in OECD countries. [OECD report](https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/9bf0cb7f-en.pdf).]

Before viewing the chart in the solution,
sketch your prediction (either on paper or in your mind).

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Think about what trend you would expect to see in this dataset.
[Do you think countries with a high percentage of heavy drinkers
have high or low remaining life expectancy at age 65?]{.slide-bullet}

```{python}
#| label: fig-polar
#| slide-show: output
#| echo: false
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

income_df = pd.read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

correct = alt.Chart(income_df, title='A').mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    tooltip=['country', 'income_group', 'region']
)

flipped = (
    correct
    .transform_calculate(life_expectancy_at_65=6+alt.expr.abs(18-alt.datum['life_expectancy_at_65']))
    .properties(title='B')
)
correct | flipped
```

::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}


That may not be the pattern you expected!
In this dataset, countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers
tend to have higher remaining life expectancy at age 65.
The chart has shown us an association,
but it hasn't explained why the two measures move together.
What might be missing from the picture?

:::

::::

:::::

Did the pattern above match your expectations?
Proceed to the next exercise
to find out if there is more to this dataset than meets the eye!

::::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

An unexpected pattern is a good reason to look more closely,
not a reason to jump to a conclusion.
Could another variable be related to both measures?
The table below gives us a few clues.
You can also hover over the points in the previous chart
to find out more about each country.

```{python}
#| label: income-data-preview
#| echo: false
show_df(income_df[['country', 'region', 'income_group', 'percentage_heavy_drinkers', 'life_expectancy_at_65']])
```

Study the table and the tooltips in the previous chart.
What do you think might be the reason
that countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers
also have higher remaining life expectancy at age 65?
Suggest one visual change to the chart
that would help you explore whether your suggested reason
could influence the relationship between alcohol consumption and life expectancy.

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Could other variables in the dataset be related to both alcohol consumption and life expectancy?
For example, consider the country's income group or world region.
Could you group the points by one of these variables using shape or color?

::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

Both a country's income group and its region
might help explain differences in alcohol consumption and life expectancy.
Here, we will explore income group only; you can explore region on your own.
To add this information to the chart,
we could use different colors to group the points visually by income group:

```{python}
#| label: income-groups-revealed
#| slide-show: output
#| slide-title: What changes when we group by income?
#| echo: false
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    color='income_group',
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
)
```

Notice how the data points form clusters by income group.
Coloring reveals that both the percentage of heavy drinkers
and remaining life expectancy at age 65 are associated with income group.
**High-income countries** tend to have higher values for both measures.
We see the opposite picture for most **low-income countries**, where both measures are lower.

This gives us a possible explanation for the surprising overall trend.
[Income level could be a [confounding variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confounding)]{.slide-bullet},
influencing both alcohol consumption and life expectancy.
The chart suggests this possibility but does not establish those causal effects.
Crucially, the points represent **countries, not people**:
we cannot conclude that the people who drink heavily
are the same people who live longer.
We would need individual-level data and an appropriate study design
to investigate that relationship.

The data hasn't changed, but our view of it has.
Grouping turns a puzzling overall trend into a more granular question:
does the relationship hold within comparable groups?

:::

::::

:::::

## The two main purposes of grouping

As we have seen in the exercises above, grouping can have major benefits.
We can divide these benefits into two main categories,
both of which help us arrive at more accurate conclusions about our data:

::: {.slide-bullet}

1. **Directly compare** observations between groups.
2. **Reveal patterns** within individual groups that are obscured
   when viewing the data from all groups together.

:::

These benefits are often connected and can be explored simultaneously.
When we grouped the alcohol consumption data by income level,
the positive relationship in the pooled data was much less apparent within groups.
Grouping also made it easier to compare
observations between groups.

### Simpson's paradox

Differences between overall and within-group relationships are central to
**Simpson's paradox** (named after the statistician Edward H. Simpson, rather than the TV series).
In the classic form of this phenomenon,
a trend within individual groups reverses when the groups are combined.
Grouping can also reveal trends that are weak or absent in the pooled data.

Below we show a simplified illustration of this aggregation effect.
Notice how the overall dataset shows little apparent relationship between X and Y,
but when the observations are colored by group,
you can see that both groups exhibit a negative trend between X and Y:
larger values of X tend to be associated with smaller values of Y, and vice versa.
This is a prime example of the utility of grouping in deepening our
understanding of a dataset; without it, we would have missed the within-group relationships.

::: {.panel-tabset .slide-columns}

### Overall {.slide-fragment .slide-with-content}

```{python}
#| label: simpsons-ungrouped
#| slide-show: output
#| echo: false
simpsons_df = pd.read_csv("data/simpsons_paradox_data_l.csv")
alt.Chart(simpsons_df).mark_point().encode(
  x='X',
  y='Y',
)
```

### By group {.slide-fragment .slide-with-content}

```{python}
#| label: simpsons-grouped
#| slide-show: output
#| echo: false
alt.Chart(simpsons_df).mark_point().encode(
  color='Group',
  x='X',
  y='Y',
)
```

:::

## What type of column can we use for grouping?

In general, we are interested in [grouping data by "categorical" columns]{.slide-bullet}.
If there is a natural order to the categories (e.g., education levels
or letter grades), we can be more precise and call the column "ordinal".
If there is no such order,
we say that the column is "nominal" (e.g., types of fruit or color names).
As a general rule, we will not group data by quantitative columns
that hold continuous data (e.g., height or age), but there are exceptions.
For example, we might turn ages recorded in whole years into categories
that we can group by, such as 18–24, 25–34, and 35–44.

[**Ordinal**: a natural order to the categories (e.g., education levels
or letter grades)]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs" .slide-subbullet}
[**Nominal**: no order (e.g., types of fruit or color names)]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs" .slide-subbullet}
[Don't group data by quantitative columns
that hold continuous data (e.g., height or age)]{.slide-bullet}

## Channels for grouping

Generally speaking, position
and color are the two most effective visual channels to use for grouping.
Shape can also be used,
but often either in combination with one of the other two or
for a specific purpose.

:::: {.slide-visual .slide-columns slide-widths="40,60"}

![Classical ordering of static identity channels for grouping; effectiveness depends on the task and design. Adapted from [Visualization Analysis and Design](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~tmm/vadbook/figures.html), Tamara Munzner, with illustrations by Eamonn Maguire (2014, CC BY 4.0); motion omitted.](img/grouping-channels.svg){#fig-grouping-channels width=451.2 fig-alt="Three grouping channels in classical order: spatial region illustrated by separate clusters, color hue by interleaved colored points, and shape by interleaved circles, squares, and triangles."}

::::

Let's take a look at a familiar example: the traffic light.
Do you think that traffic lights are well designed?
At first glance,
their use of red and green presents a challenge for people with red–green color vision deficiency.
Thankfully,
signals can communicate their meaning through position and shape as well as color,
as in the pedestrian signals below.

::: {.slide-fragment slide-title='Which are used in a traffic light?'}

![Traffic lights often use color, shape, and position to communicate meaning. <a href="https://www.vecteezy.com/vector-art/80397127-pedestrian-traffic-light-signals-with-green-walk-and-red-stop-hand-flat-icons">Pedestrian Vectors by Achmad Saroju via Vecteezy</a>](img/traffic-light.svg){#fig-traffic-light width=451.2 fig-alt="Illustration of pedestrian traffic light with a green and red person and different positions."}

:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Shape up**

Some regions also use shape to distinguish traffic signals for cars, as in this example from Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.

![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/Colourblind_traffic_signal.JPG)

:::

Using several visual channels for the same distinction gives viewers more than one cue to interpret.
Even traffic signals for cars that lack distinct shapes typically use a consistent arrangement,
so drivers can use position as well as color to distinguish the signals.

### Applying grouping strategies

The grammar of graphics allows
for the grouping strategies
to be conveniently defined via an easily interchangeable syntax:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language" .slide-columns}

:::: {.slide-fragment}

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Color

```{.python}
encode(color='category_column')
```

#### Shape

```{.python}
encode(shape='category_column')
```

#### Position

```{.python}
encode(x='category_column')
```

```{.python}
encode(y='category_column')
```

:::

::::

:::: {.slide-fragment}
::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Color

```{.r}
aes(color = category_column)
```

#### Shape

```{.r}
aes(shape = category_column)
```

#### Position

```{.r}
aes(x = category_column)
```

```{.r}
aes(y = category_column)
```
:::

### Color

[The human brain can detect color differences with little cognitive effort]{.slide-bullet}.
[Color is a **preattentive feature**]{.slide-bullet}^[Wolfe JM, Utochkin IS.
What is a preattentive feature?
Curr Opin Psychol. 2019 Oct;29:19-26. doi: 10.1016/j.copsyc.2018.11.005.
Epub 2018 Nov 13.
PMID: 30472539; PMCID: PMC6513732.] which means
that the brain can tell apart colors even without conscious attention.
This is heightened when there is a high contrast,
such as between the complementary colors blue and orange.

This is great news for grouping!
By encoding our categorical variable as color,
we can leverage the brain's ability to infer groups.
Conveniently, [color doesn't alter the layout
or structure]{.slide-bullet} of the data visualization,
so [it's an efficient way to compare the exact values of data points between
groups]{.slide-bullet}.

In the second exercise of this chapter, we already saw how color could be used to
group our life expectancy data by income group.
Let's now see what the code to create this chart looks like:

[Avoid using more than 4-6 colors]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs" .slide-bullet}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

:::: {.slide-bullet}

What explanation would you suggest for this pattern?

::::

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

Here we use `color='income_group'`:

```{python}
#| label: income-color-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Color — Altair
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd


income_df = pd.read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Here we use `color = income_group`:

```{r}
#| label: grouping-tidyverse-setup
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# Tidyverse is so noisy when imported the first time, so let's do it here in silence
library(tidyverse)
options(readr.show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: income-color-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Color — ggplot
library(tidyverse)

income_df <- read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

ggplot(income_df, aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group
    )) +
    geom_point()
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

#### Avoid using color for more than 5–7 groups {.slide-skip}

<!-- TODO add an example with too many colors and then include this insteadof note on first color page -->

Using too many colors or colors
that are too similar can blur the differences between groups.
There are also several other important aspects of using colors effectively,
such as how to ensure accessibility,
particularly for people with color vision deficiencies.
We will learn more about these topics in a later chapter,
but for now it's enough to remember that
when there are more than about 5–7 groups in the data,
it might be better to break it down into separate charts instead of grouping by
color.

:::

### Shape

[Shape is a less effective grouping strategy on its own]{.slide-bullet},
but [it can be combined with color to provide an additional visual cue]{.slide-bullet}.

The syntax for mapping a variable to the shape channel is similar to that for color:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: income-shape-alt
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='income_group'
)
```

Setting `filled=True` fills all the points with a solid color,
making the shapes easier to distinguish:

```{python}
#| label: income-filled-shape-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Combining shape and color — altair
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(filled=True).encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='income_group'
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: income-shape-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Combining shape and color — ggplot
ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group,
        shape = income_group
    ) +
    geom_point()
```

:::

While this combined approach can make grouping clearer, there are some pitfalls. For instance, hollow symbols limit the total area that can be colored, reducing the impact of color. Filled shapes can make color easier to see when combining shape and color.
Additionally, smaller shapes are difficult to distinguish, so when plotting a dense scatterplot of small marks, try restricting the number of unique shapes to three or fewer, or consider avoiding using shape altogether.
<!--TODO number of shapes -->

::: {.callout-warning}

#### Avoid using color and shape for different variables

It is often difficult to interpret charts that map one variable to `color`
and another to `shape`.
This tends to lead to too much visual information
and it is difficult to distinguish the many different combinations visually.

The many combinations of income group
and region in this chart are hard to separate visually,
which makes this chart ineffective:
<!-- TODO Include background coloring to clearly identify ineffective examples? Too similar to Fundamentals of Data Visualization? -->

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: income-region-alt
#| slide-show: output
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(filled=True).encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='region'
)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: income-region-gg
ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group,
        shape = region
    ) +
    geom_point()
```

::::


:::

::: {.callout-warning}

#### Avoid using size to group by a categorical variable

Size is often used to represent the magnitude of quantitative data.
Under limited circumstances,
it can also be used for grouping data according to a categorical variable,
but in general this is best avoided.

Since size has an inherent direction from small to large,
it works better for ordinal than nominal categorical data.
One example is the World Bank income levels, ranging from low to high.
However, even when used for ordinal data,
it is often difficult to tell different
sizes apart, as you can see in the chart below.

```{python}
#| label: income-size-alt
#| slide-show: output
#| echo: false
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(color='#FF0039').encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    size='income_group',
)
```

:::

### Position {.slide-skip}

#### X and Y position

[Grouping by position often creates the clearest separation between groups]{.slide-bullet}.
Distributing the groups along the x- or y-axis gives each group its own visual lane,
preventing observations from different groups from overlapping.
However, [the grouping column now occupies one positional visual channel]{.slide-bullet},
so [there is only one positional channel left]{.slide-bullet}
for encoding the values we want to compare between the groups.

Below, we distribute the regions along the y-axis.
This leaves us with a choice of whether to use the x-axis
for `percentage_heavy_drinkers` or `life_expectancy_at_65`.
We cannot represent both quantitative variables with position in this chart.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}


```{python}
#| label: region-position-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Giving each group its own lane — Altair
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='region',
)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: region-position-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Giving each group its own lane — ggplot
ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = region,
    ) +
    geom_point()
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

##### Avoid rotated category labels along the x-axis

We could swap the x and y variables above,
but then the region labels would be rotated and harder to read.
Short category labels that fit horizontally can work well on the x-axis.
For longer labels, placing the categories on the y-axis usually makes the text easier to read.

```{python}
#| label: region-position-alt-xy-swap
#| slide-show: output
#| echo: false
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(color='#FF0039').encode(
    x='region',
    y='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
)
```

:::

#### Faceting

Faceting takes the concept of grouping to the next level.
Instead of using different visual channels within a single chart,
[generates multiple charts (or "facets"),
each dedicated to a grouped subset of the data]{.slide-bullet}.
Faceting is [particularly effective for highlighting distinct trends
and patterns within each subset]{.slide-bullet},
as well as identifying extreme values or outliers within groups.
We could think of faceting as a type of position grouping,
but its advantage is that it [keeps both the x- and y-axes free
for other variables]{.slide-bullet}.

[Previous grouping strategies can be used within each facet]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs" .slide-bullet}

Let's create a separate facet for each income group,
so that the relationship between `percentage_heavy_drinkers`
and `life_expectancy_at_65` within each group stands out.
We can lay out the facets differently depending on what we are most
interested in comparing.
If the y-axis is the primary channel
for comparison, we would spread the facets out horizontally in a single row.
If the x-axis is the primary channel
for comparison, we would spread the facets out vertically in a single column.
In either case, the scales should be shared for direct comparisons.
Neither axis is our sole focus here:
we are interested in comparing the overall pattern within each group,
so we will lay out the facets in a compact grid to save space.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

To facet by income group, we can append `.facet('income_group')` to our chart.
We create a 2 × 2 grid of facets by using the `columns` parameter.

```{python}
#| label: income-facets-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Faceting by income — Altair
alt.Chart(income_df, height=250, width=250).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
).facet(
    'income_group',
    columns=2
)
```

In addition to faceting on a single variable in the data,
faceting can also be done over two variables:
one spread horizontally and one spread out vertically in the faceted charts.
In Altair, we would use the `column`
and `row` parameters to achieve this.
For example, to have facets that are grouped by both income group and region,
we could use `facet(column='income_group', row='region')`.
This can be effective when we need to group our data further,
but it can make the chart difficult to take in at a glance,
so it is best used when there are fewer categories in the faceting variables.

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

To facet by income group,
we can add `+ facet_wrap(vars(income_group))` to our chart.
The `vars()` function specifies which columns to use for faceting,
just as `aes()` specifies the mappings from variables to visual channels.

By default, `facet_wrap()` arranges these four groups in a 2 × 2 grid,
which is appropriate for our visualization.
Here, we set the `ncol` argument explicitly to illustrate how you can control
the number of columns in the facet grid.

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: income-facets-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Faceting by income — ggplot
ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65
    ) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(vars(income_group), ncol = 2)
```

In addition to faceting on a single variable in the data,
faceting can also be done over two variables:
one spread horizontally and one spread out vertically in the faceted charts.
In ggplot, we would replace `facet_wrap()` with `facet_grid()` to do this.
For example, to have facets that are grouped by both income group and region,
we could use `facet_grid(rows = vars(region), cols = vars(income_group))`.
This can be effective when we need to group our data further,
but it can make the chart difficult to take in at a glance,
so it is best used when there are fewer categories in the faceting variables.

:::

As you can see above, faceting makes it easier to observe the overall pattern for each income group and how tightly clustered the values are. It also reveals potential outliers in the upper-middle-income facet: we can easily spot two countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers than the others in that group. On the other hand, it is now harder to compare individual values between groups because the points are spread across different charts instead of being close together in a single chart.

All the previous grouping strategies can be used within each facet as additional layers of grouping. This nested grouping can be useful for dividing our data according to multiple categorical variables, but it can become confusing if we try to fit too much into a single visualization. How many grouping variables you can use depends on how well separated the groups are and how many observations you have. More observations and less separation between groups mean that you need to be more careful and may need fewer layers of grouping to keep the visualization easy to interpret.

Let's try out an example of how we can use faceting together with other grouping strategies.

::::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

Edit this chart to use both faceting and color for grouping.
Facet by world region (`region`) and color the points by World Bank income group (`income_group`).
Ensure that only two facets are shown per row.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{pyodide}

import pandas as pd
from utils import assert_chart_equal

url = 'data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv'
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: facet-python-exercise

)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{webr fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: facet-exercise-r-setup
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - facet_ggplot
library(ggplot2)

url <- 'data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv'
```

```{webr fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: facet-r-exercise
#| exercise: facet_ggplot
income_df <- readr::read_csv(url, show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
    ) +
    geom_point()
```

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: region-facets-alt
alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group'
).facet(
    'region',
    columns=2
)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
#| label: region-facets-gg
ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group
    ) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(vars(region), ncol = 2)
```
